---
title: "Methodology and Conventions"
format: html
---

## Observation calendar

Daily source prices are filtered to the configured inclusive date range and asset set
before validation. Weekly profiles use one Friday valuation calendar for all assets.
For each cutoff the last quote dated on or before that Friday is used, with a maximum
configured age of zero to four calendar days. A missing whole week is an error; the
engine never compresses two weeks into one return or uses a future quote. A trailing
week whose Friday falls after the configured end is excluded. Daily profiles retain
common observed trading dates.

The valuation audit records each cutoff, asset, quote date, quote age and price. Weekly
valuation labels are exactly seven days apart, even when individual markets close on
different holidays. This is a daily-close convention, not an intraday synchronization
model. Synthetic fixtures use Friday dates and are explicitly labelled as software
verification inputs.

## Portfolio returns and signed risk

Portfolio simple return is the weighted sum of asset simple returns. Portfolio log
return is `log1p(portfolio_simple_return)`; weighted asset log returns are not substituted
for it. Forecasts and observations use the same configured return space. Fixed weights
imply rebalancing at each observation, with trading costs outside the present model.
Local-index-return mode performs no FX conversion. Base-currency mode requires aligned
FX returns quoted as base-currency units per unit of asset currency.

For signed return $r$, define loss $L=-r$. At confidence $c$, VaR is the $c$ quantile of
loss, and ES averages the worst $1-c$ probability mass. The signed outputs `loss_var`
and `loss_es` are used for scoring and exceptions. They can be negative if even the
relevant tail earns a gain. The nonnegative `var` and `es` fields are display magnitudes
and do not replace signed forecasts in evaluation.

For empirical ES, losses are sorted from largest to smallest. The largest
$\lfloor n(1-c)\rfloor$ observations receive full weight, and the next receives the
fractional remainder. Dividing their weighted sum by $n(1-c)$ integrates exactly the
tail mass, including samples with ties and samples smaller than $1/(1-c)$. A strict
threshold subset is not used to approximate this integral.

## Marginals, dependence and benchmark design

Marginal fits must converge and satisfy parameter checks. Residual and squared-residual
Ljung–Box diagnostics screen autocorrelation before AIC/BIC ranking. If no candidate
passes all diagnostic screens, the best valid converged fallback is selected with a
warning. PIT KS/AD statistics and conventional p-values remain exploratory because
the same observations estimated the marginal parameters. A calibrated PIT test would
require a refit-aware bootstrap or an independently validated forecast sample.

The native two-step marginal engine is an approximation; its information criteria
are compared only within the restricted ARMA order. Production-package and native
engine identities are retained in the outputs. PIT values are clipped inside $(0,1)$
for numerical inverse-CDF evaluation, with clipping counts retained in diagnostics.

Copula tail coefficients use the return-CDF scale. Lower-tail dependence concerns
joint extreme losses, and upper-tail dependence concerns joint extreme gains.
Simulation transforms joint uniforms through the fitted marginals, restores their
conditional means and volatilities, and aggregates in simple-return space before
converting to the configured portfolio return space.

Simple benchmarks are supplemented by a fixed univariate portfolio sGARCH(1,1)
Student-t model. Optional independence, Gaussian, Student-t and BB1 ablations reuse
the same selected and refitted asset marginals at each origin. This separates evidence
about dependence from improvements due to conditional volatility or heavy tails.
A fixed-family ablation that cannot fit is a recorded failure, not a different copula.

## Rolling evaluation and missing forecasts

At origin $t$, only observations through $t$ are available; the forecast is scored on
the next valuation. Moving or expanding windows and periodic specification selection
are explicit configuration choices. Selected specifications are refitted at every
origin. Checkpoints include input, configuration and implementation identities so that
incompatible states cannot be silently resumed.

Forecast-date/model/confidence keys must be unique, and compared models must have the
same realised return for a given date. Failed and missing forecasts remain visible.
Coverage describes the available observations on each model's full forecast calendar;
independence transitions are not bridged across missing forecasts. An unidentified
boundary-case independence statistic is not represented as proof of independence.

Quantile loss compares signed VaR forecasts. Ranking uses a common set of dates with
valid scores for every model at the same confidence level. Joint VaR/ES scores use
their own common set, with counts and availability reported separately. The rank is
an ordering of observed mean losses, not a hypothesis test or a composite of p-values,
complexity and runtime.

## Expected Shortfall scoring and uncertainty

The implemented Fissler–Ziegel zero-homogeneous score is

$$
S(L,v,e)=\frac{\max(L-v,0)}{(1-c)e}+\frac{v}{e}+\log(e)-1,
\qquad e>0,\quad e\geq v.
$$

Lower is better when comparing forecasts on the same observations and confidence
level. Signed VaR may be negative. A valid forecast whose signed ES is nonpositive
is outside this particular score's domain and receives an unavailable score; the
forecast itself is neither clipped nor silently reclassified. Descriptive tail
residuals are also reported, but they are not a formal ES hypothesis test.

Paired predictive comparisons share the eligible dates across all models at each
confidence level and score type. Loss differences are model minus reference, so
negative values favour the model. A circular block bootstrap, using blocks of
$\lceil n^{1/3}\rceil$ observations by default, reports a percentile interval and a
centred two-sided bootstrap p-value. Holm adjustment applies across the comparisons
in the call; percentile intervals remain marginal rather than simultaneous.

Inference requires at least 20 paired observations and at least two blocks. Internal
gaps in the common calendar make bootstrap inference unavailable rather than allowing
resampled blocks to bridge missing forecasts. The point difference, common-sample
fraction and inference status remain visible, and per-date score differences are saved.
A point improvement, especially with an interval crossing zero, is not established
superiority. Coverage tests also have limited power when the expected number of tail
exceptions is small. Evaluation-period selection and multiple comparisons limit how
broadly any favourable result can be interpreted.

Monte Carlo repeats across seeds estimate simulation error conditional on fitted
parameters. They do not quantify parameter, model-selection or regime uncertainty.
The seed, simulation budget, RNG kind and chunk size are part of the run identity.

## Reproduction and interpretation

Each run records source revision and dirty state, implementation/configuration/input
hashes, the valuation interval, software versions and simulation settings. A local
run archive retains the price snapshot, configuration and session information.
Output hashes tie generated tables and figures to their manifest; the report refuses
to combine absent or mismatched artefacts.

Software tests establish implemented invariants, while real-data out-of-sample
experiments assess forecast behaviour. Neither is sufficient on its own to establish
an investable production risk system. This demonstration remains bivariate, and its
default local-index-return example omits FX hedging, transaction costs and market
microstructure effects.
